place.zh: 图书馆 · 古籍部 · 冬至夜
place.en: The library · the rare-books room · the winter solstice night

setup.zh: 加时赢了三分，没有一分是他的；大刘「第二个，是你自己投的」。冬至默写九条，蛋账「清」。冬至夜守恒温机，他在古籍部的黑里先怕，后听，吐两口气看着自己的心慢下来，数清了自己的心跳。
setup.en: They win overtime by three, none of it his; Big Liu: "the second one you shot yourself." Nine meridians at the solstice dictation; the egg debt "settled." Watching the climate unit on the solstice night, in the dark of the rare-books room he is afraid first, then listens, breathes out twice and watches his own heart slow, and counts his own heartbeat.

recap.en: Winter solstice night, sitting still. Heard it.

zh: 六十一；两指一搭：六十二。
en: Sixty-one; two fingers on the wrist: sixty-two.
"Winter solstice night, sitting still. Heard it."

story.zh:
加时五分钟，针推赢了三分，没有一分是他的。他罚完球就被换了下来，坐在替补席上，手里攥着那只翻过来的纸杯，一直攥到终场。大刘坐在他旁边，脚脖子上敷着冰袋，每进一个球，就拿拳头砸一下他的大腿。终场哨响，大刘拿胳膊勾住他的脖子，喘着说了一句这一个学期对他说过的最长的话：「第二个，是你自己投的。」老蔡从看台上翻下来，举着那块「沈道友稳」在场边跑了一圈，被保安拦了回去。

阿禾在场边记完了最后一行，合上本子，往他这边看了一眼，什么也没说，点了一下头。然后她收拾替补席，一只一只把纸杯收进垃圾袋，收到最末那一只，攥成一团的那一只，她看了一眼，没扔，展平了，揣进羽绒服口袋。雷老师从记录台后头绕过来，把比赛用球往他怀里一塞：「给零号。」

人散得差不多了。马小宝坐在新地板上解鞋带，冲他笑：「没事。家里还有。」那只手在鞋带上绕了两回，没解开。第三回，手停在半空，他往后一仰，倒在了地板上。

不是摔，是软的，像一袋粮食从车斗上滑下来。

沈芒离他四步。四步里他想起的不是哪一课，是停电那一夜黑地里那只腕子：快得数不过来，中间空一下。他跪下去，两根指头按在马小宝脖子上——一跳赶着一跳，像有人在里头拿拳头擂门，擂着擂着，空一下。马小宝眼睛还睁着，嘴唇是灰的：「……心……要蹦出来了……」

「雷老师！打120！」他的嗓子劈了，「门口墙上那个黄箱子——阿禾！」

阿禾手里的垃圾袋已经扔了，人往门口跑，马尾甩了起来。

沈芒把马小宝两条腿架到自己膝盖上，俯下身，脸对着他的脸：「小宝哥，你看着我。先别吸气，往外吐，吐得比吸的长，一直吐到底。」他自己先吐，吐得长长的，跟罚球线上那一口一样。马小宝跟着吐，吐一半就喘；他不催，一口一口地领，跟停电那一夜一样。指头一直没离开那根脖子：数不过来——还是数不过来——数得过来了。十秒，二十三下。又十秒，十九下。

阿禾跪在另一边，拆开黄箱子，贴片一左一右贴上去。机器说话了，一个平平的女声：「正在分析心律，请不要接触病人。」所有人的手都抬了起来。「不建议电击。」

救护车来的时候，那颗心在沈芒的指头底下慢了下来，还是快，可一下是一下了。担架抬起来，随车的大夫问：「吃过什么没有？」

马小宝看着沈芒。

沈芒张了张嘴。停电那一夜他说过：黑成这样，我什么也没看见。

「……他吃过一个白瓶子里的药，」他说，「瓶子上全是洋文。他书包里还有一个棕色的瓶子。」

马小宝把眼睛闭上了。担架出了门。

二十日，他又去古籍部，请葛奶奶把那一函《养性延命录》捧出来。「长息」那一页的页脚还有一行铅笔字，比别处都淡：「冬至夜，静坐。不见。」铅笔到这儿就断了，后头一个字也没有。他把函还了，抽出手札的头一册，这回从头一页读起：漏勺，坠谷，鹅毛；翻过一页，是一条他没读过的：「十三岁秋，随舅舅南行。蒙山之南，泗水之上，有观。」他在这一条上停了一会儿，把书塞回函里。

冬至是礼拜二。上午严老师调了课，来上期末前最后一回复习，照本宣科讲完了，照例下课前默写：十二正经，写名字，写走向。九月里头一回默写，他交的是白卷。这一回，他写出了九条。有一条写串了，把手太阴肺经一路画到了脚上。严老师拿红笔在旁边批了四个字：「想象力好。」又在卷子顶上写了个分数，不高，可是有。他对着那四个红字，脸绿了又白。眼镜看了那条线，倒说了句公道话：「你这不算全错，是抄近道。」沈芒把卷子叠好揣进兜里。九条是九条，九月里是零条。

中午一食堂吃饺子，队从楼梯口排到门外。他在阿禾对面坐下，没动筷子，先从兜里往外掏钱：一张十块，一张五块，一张一块，一个五毛的钢镚，两个一毛的。他一样一样排在桌上，排成一溜，又在兜里摸了半天，摸出一张公交卡、一张饭卡、一团纸——是早上那张卷子。「十六块七，」他说，「差一毛。」九月那笔蛋账，补测那天就免了，他照样还。阿禾低头看着那一溜钱，往前翻到九月那一行，把钱一样一样收进一个小信封；那一毛，她没提。然后她在那一行末尾写了一个字：「清。」写完了，夹起一个饺子，蘸了醋，吃了。沈芒认识她一个学期，她连他厕所去了几趟都数；这是他头一回看见，她放过了一毛钱。

他八点到古籍部。葛奶奶正往墙上贴一张纸，纸上一枝梅花，九朵，每朵九瓣，一瓣也没涂。她拿红铅笔，在头一朵的头一瓣上细细涂满了：「九九消寒图。冬至起数九，一天涂一瓣，八十一瓣涂完，河也开了，柳也绿了。」她坐下来倒了两杯热水。沈芒帮她干活：每到整点，去墙角看一眼那台机器的表，温度、湿度，各记一个数。记着记着，他觉得自己有点像阿禾。

十点，她起身往里屋走，到门口回头：「看不见的东西，别使劲看。先听。」

他取下一部《奇经八脉考》，翻到一句：「内景隧道，惟反观者能照察之」。内景，是身子里头的景；往里头看的人，才照得见。可往里看，拿什么看？他合上书，没想出来。十一点半，他关了台灯。

黑得没有边。

先是什么也没有。脑子里倒热闹得很：那个罚球在筐上转的那一圈半，阿禾本子上那个「清」，马小宝绕了两回没解开的鞋带，眼镜说的「抄近道」——一样接一样，像有人在他脑子里放幻灯片。放着放着，换了一张：十一月那个停电的夜，也是这间屋子，也是这么黑，黑里头另一个人的喘。那一夜怕黑的是马小宝。这一回，只有他一个。

这念头一起，他的后背先凉了。四面是看不见的书架，书架后头是看不见的墙，墙外头是土。黑是有分量的，一层一层压过来，压在胸口上。他的喘一下子浅了，快了。

先听。

头一样听见的，是恒温机。一起，一伏。听得久了，听出来它不是一直一个声：起的时候高一点，伏的时候低一点，中间夹着一下很轻的「嗒」。第二样，是自己的喘：吸进去凉，吐出来暖。第三样，他起先以为还是恒温机——一下很闷的、很软的「咚」，不在耳朵外头，在胸口里头，一下，一下，比恒温机快得多。

他没摸腕子，可他知道那是什么。方才那一阵怕，原来全在这儿。

他没去管那份怕，只照着罚球线上那样，长长地吐了一口气，又吐了一口。那一下一下的「咚」，在他吐气的时候，过了好一阵，一下比一下松，一下比一下慢，像一个跑急了的人，慢慢走了下来。他从来没有这么清楚地，看着自己的心慢下来。

黑还是那么黑，可是不压人了。

他想试一试，往里听，听得准不准。他摸黑把手机掏出来，眯着眼设了一分钟，屏幕朝下扣在桌上。不摸腕子，只听，一下，两下，三下……手机一震：五十八。再设一分钟，两根指头搭在腕子上老老实实数：六十三。差五下。

他不急着再数，先吐两口气，把脑子里那些幻灯片吐干净了，再去听。那「咚」从胸口里浮上来，清楚了一些。手机一震：六十一。搭腕子：六十二。差一下。

头一回他是在猜，这一回，他是真听见了。

他把老蔡枕头里捏的一根绒毛搁在上嘴唇上，毛尖刚好挨着鼻孔底下，吐得很慢，很细，细到那口气像是从身子里一点一点渗出去的。九月里，就是这样一根毛，一口气吹得飞出了窗缝。它没动。他又吐了一口。它还是没动。

后来，闭着的眼前是一层极细的灰，灰里有一点亮，很小，偏上一点，不闪，不灭。他睁开眼，屋子是黑的，什么也没有；闭上眼，它还在那儿。他没去追，也没去想它是什么，只听了听自己的心：不快，不慢。一个人在地底下，黑里头冒出一点来路不明的亮，换了九月里的他，早吓得去摸灯了。他这会儿一点也不怕，倒像在黑地里碰见了一个认得的人。

天快亮时，他在备忘录里写：「冬至夜，静坐。听见了。」葛奶奶送到门口：「你方才在黑里头，喘得又急又浅，后来又不喘了。」沈芒一愣：「您没睡着？」「我七十二了，睡不实。」她把门推开一条缝，「前头那个，也是这样坐了一宿。他出来的时候，脸色没你好。」他还想问前头那个是谁，门已经合上了。

外头天还没亮。图书馆的台阶底下，蹲着一团红黄的东西，脑门上一撮毛立着，不知在这冷地里候了多久。它一见他，站起来抖了抖身上的霜，不叫，走过来，把脑袋往他手心里一拱。他蹲下来，摸了摸它的头。手心里是热的。
story.en:
Five minutes of overtime; Acupuncture and Tuina won by three, and not a single point was his. He was subbed off the moment the free throws were done and sat on the bench clutching the turned-over cup until the final whistle. Big Liu sat beside him with an ice pack on his ankle, and every time a shot went in he punched Shen Mang in the thigh. At the whistle Big Liu hooked an arm round his neck and, still panting, said the longest thing he'd said to him all semester: "The second one — that one you shot yourself." Old Cai came tumbling down out of the stands and ran a lap of the sideline holding up "Steady, Daoist Friend Shen," until a security guard turned him back.

Ahe finished her last line at the sideline, closed the notebook, looked over at him, said nothing, and gave a single nod. Then she cleared the bench, dropping the paper cups one by one into a rubbish bag; when she got to the last one, the one crushed into a ball, she looked at it, didn't throw it away, smoothed it flat, and tucked it into the pocket of her down jacket. Coach Lei came round from behind the scorer's table and pushed the game ball into his arms: "For Number Zero."

The crowd had mostly gone. Ma Xiaobao sat on the new floor untying his laces and grinned at him: "No problem. There's more at home." His hand went round the lace twice and didn't get it undone. The third time, the hand stopped in mid-air, and he tipped back and lay down on the floor.

It wasn't a fall. It was soft, like a sack of grain sliding off the back of a truck.

Shen Mang was four steps away. In those four steps what came to him wasn't any lesson; it was the wrist in the dark on the night of the blackout: too fast to count, dropping one in the middle. He knelt and pressed two fingers to Ma Xiaobao's neck — one beat chasing the next, like someone inside pounding on a door with a fist, pounding and pounding, then a gap. Ma Xiaobao's eyes were still open, his lips grey: "…my heart… it's jumping out…"

"Coach Lei! Call 120!" His voice cracked. "The yellow box on the wall by the door — Ahe!"

Ahe had already dropped the rubbish bag and was running for the door, her ponytail flying.

Shen Mang lifted Ma Xiaobao's legs onto his own knees and bent down, face to face: "Xiaobao, look at me. Don't breathe in yet — breathe out, longer than you breathe in, all the way out." He breathed out first himself, long, the same breath as on the free-throw line. Ma Xiaobao followed, and gasped halfway; Shen Mang didn't hurry him, led him one breath at a time, the same as on the night of the blackout. His fingers never left that neck: too fast to count — still too fast — countable now. Ten seconds, twenty-three beats. Another ten seconds, nineteen.

Ahe knelt on the other side, opened the yellow box and stuck the pads on, one left, one right. The machine spoke, a flat woman's voice: "Analysing heart rhythm. Do not touch the patient." Every hand came up. "No shock advised."

By the time the ambulance came the heart under Shen Mang's fingers had slowed — still fast, but one beat was one beat now. As the stretcher came up, the doctor with it asked: "Has he taken anything?"

Ma Xiaobao looked at Shen Mang.

Shen Mang opened his mouth. On the night of the blackout he had said: dark as this, I didn't see a thing.

"…He's been taking pills from a white bottle," he said. "It's all foreign writing. There's a brown bottle in his bag too."

Ma Xiaobao closed his eyes. The stretcher went out of the door.

On the 20th he went back to the rare-books room and asked Granny Ge to bring out the case of *Records of Nourishing Nature and Prolonging Life*. At the foot of the "long breath" page there was one more line of pencil, fainter than all the rest: "Winter solstice night, sat in stillness. Did not see." The pencil broke off there, and after it not a word. He handed the case back, drew out the first volume of the journal and this time read it from the first page: the leaky ladle, the gorge, the goose feather; over the page was an entry he had never read: "Age thirteen, autumn. Went south with my uncle. South of Mount Meng, on the River Si, there stands a Daoist temple." He stayed on that line a while, then slid the book back into the case.

The winter solstice fell on a Tuesday. In the morning Teacher Yan had rescheduled, for the last review before finals; he lectured straight from the book as always, and as always, before the bell, dictation: the twelve regular meridians, names and courses. In the first dictation in September he had handed in a blank sheet. This time he wrote out nine. One of them went astray: he ran the Hand Taiyin Lung meridian all the way down to the foot. Teacher Yan wrote four characters beside it in red: "Good imagination." And at the top, a mark — low, but a mark. He stared at the red characters, and his face went green, then white. Specs looked at the stray line and said something fair: "That's not all wrong. That's a shortcut." Shen Mang folded the sheet and put it in his pocket. Nine is nine; in September it was zero.

At noon the First Canteen served dumplings, the queue running from the stairs out the door. He sat down opposite Ahe, didn't touch his chopsticks, and started pulling money out of his pockets: a ten, a five, a one, a fifty-fen coin, two ten-fen coins. He laid them out on the table in a row, dug around in his pockets a while longer, and came up with a bus card, a meal card and a wad of paper — the morning's dictation. "Sixteen seventy," he said. "Ten fen short." The September egg debt had been waived the day of the retest; he was paying it anyway. Ahe looked down at the row of money, turned back to the September line, and gathered the money piece by piece into a small envelope; the ten fen, she didn't mention. Then at the end of that line she wrote one word: "Settled." That done, she picked up a dumpling, dipped it in vinegar, and ate it. He had known her a semester; she counted even his trips to the toilet. This was the first time he'd seen her let ten fen go.

He got to the rare-books room at eight. Granny Ge was pinning a sheet of paper to the wall: a branch of plum blossom, nine flowers, nine petals each, not one filled in. With a red pencil she carefully colored the first petal of the first flower: "A nine-nines cold-counting chart. From the solstice you count the nines: one petal a day, and when all eighty-one are colored the river's open and the willows are green." She sat down and poured two cups of hot water. Shen Mang helped: on the hour, every hour, he went to the corner to check the dial on the machine and write down two numbers, temperature and humidity. Writing them down, he felt a little like Ahe.

At ten she went into the back room, and turned at the door: "Things you can't see — don't strain to look at them. Listen first."

He took down a copy of the Study of the Eight Extraordinary Vessels and turned to a line: "The tunnels of the inner landscape can be illuminated only by one who looks inward." The inner landscape is the scenery inside the body; only someone looking inward can light it. But look inward with what? He closed the book without an answer. At eleven thirty, he switched off the desk lamp.

Darkness without edges.

At first there was nothing. His head, though, was crowded: the free throw rolling its lap and a half round the rim, the "Settled" in Ahe's notebook, the lace Ma Xiaobao had wound round twice without undoing, Specs's "shortcut" — one after another, like someone running a slideshow in his skull. Then the slide changed: the night of the blackout in November, this same room, this same dark, and someone else's breathing in it. That night the one afraid of the dark had been Ma Xiaobao. This time there was only him.

The thought had barely formed when his back went cold. Shelves he couldn't see on every side, walls he couldn't see behind the shelves, earth beyond the walls. The dark had weight; it came down in layers and pressed on his chest. His breathing went shallow and quick.

Listen first.

The first thing he heard was the climate unit. Rising, falling. The longer he listened, the more he heard that it wasn't one steady sound: a little higher on the rise, a little lower on the fall, and in between a very light click. The second was his own breathing: cool going in, warm coming out. The third he took at first for the unit again — a dull, soft thump, not outside his ears but inside his chest, one, one, much faster than the machine.

He didn't touch his wrist, but he knew what it was. That burst of fear a moment ago — this was where it had all been.

He left the fear alone and did what he'd done on the free-throw line: one long breath out, then another. As he breathed out, over a long while, that thump came looser each time, slower each time, like someone who has run too hard slowing to a walk. He had never watched his own heart slow down this clearly.

The dark was as dark as ever, but it no longer pressed.

He wanted to test it — listen inward, and see how accurate the listening was. He fished out his phone in the dark, squinted and set a one-minute timer, and laid it face down on the table. No wrist; just listening: one, two, three... The phone buzzed: fifty-eight. He set another minute, two fingers on his wrist this time, counting honestly: sixty-three. Five apart.

He didn't rush to count again. First two breaths out, to blow the slideshow clean, then he listened. The thump floated up out of his chest a little clearer. The phone buzzed: sixty-one. On the wrist: sixty-two. One apart.

The first time he had been guessing. This time, he had really heard it.

He set a wisp of down he'd pinched out of Old Cai's pillow on his upper lip, its tip just under his nostrils, and breathed out very slowly, very finely, so fine the breath seemed to seep out of him a little at a time. In September a wisp just like it had been blown clean out through the gap in the window on one breath. It didn't stir. He breathed out again. It still didn't stir.

Later, before his closed eyes, there was a layer of extremely fine grey, and in the grey a point of light, very small, a little above center, not flickering, not going out. He opened his eyes: the room was black, nothing there; closed them, and it was still there. He didn't chase it, and didn't wonder what it was; he only listened to his heart: not fast, not slow. Alone underground, a point of light from nowhere coming up out of the dark — the Shen Mang of September would have groped for the lamp in fright. Now he wasn't afraid at all; it felt more like running into someone he knew in the dark.

Toward dawn, he wrote in his phone notes: "Winter solstice night, sat in stillness. Heard." Granny Ge saw him to the door: "Back there in the dark, you were breathing fast and shallow, and then you weren't." Shen Mang started: "You weren't asleep?" "I'm seventy-two. I don't sleep deep." She pushed the door open a crack. "The one before you sat up all night like this too. When he came out, he didn't look as well as you." He wanted to ask who the one before was, but the door had already closed.

Outside it wasn't light yet. At the foot of the library steps crouched a reddish-yellow bundle, a tuft of fur standing up on its forehead, waiting in the cold for who knew how long. At the sight of him it stood, shook the frost off its coat, didn't bark, came over, and butted its head into his palm. He crouched and stroked its head. His palm was warm.

exits.means: the interlude ends and the story reads on
